title: Vayetze: and I knew it not (Genesis 28:16)
hook: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayetze: Jacob leaving Beer-sheba, and a town a little dimmer. Your line was people make places. Did you tell someone? Tonight, Jacob sleeps outside. Day one hundred ninety-two.

The bus stop you stand at every morning. The hallway between the kitchen and the bedroom. The stretch of highway you drive without seeing. Nobody expects anything holy there. Jacob, running from his brother, comes to an ordinary place when the sun goes down. No town, no inn. He takes one of the stones lying around, puts it under his head, and lies down on the ground to sleep. Nothing marks the spot. Today: and I knew it not.
screen: `THE BUS STOP. THE HALLWAY.` → `SUNSET, NOWHERE IN PARTICULAR.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: Jacob dreams. A ladder, a sulam, is set up on the earth, and its top reaches to heaven. Angels of God are going up and coming down on it. Up first, then down, the rabbis noticed. And God stands beside him and makes a promise: this land, children like the dust of the earth, and I will be with you and keep you wherever you go, and bring you back. Then Jacob wakes up. And he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." He's afraid, and he says the place is full of awe: nothing less than the house of God, the gate of heaven. He names it Beth-el, house of God. The text adds, almost dryly, that the town used to be called Luz. An ordinary name for an ordinary place. Now listen to that one line again. And I knew it not. The Hebrew for I here is anochi, the longer of two Hebrew words for I, and some Hasidic teachers played with it. Why didn't Jacob know God was there? Because of the anochi. Because he was full of himself, his fear, his plans, his running. The rabbis also gave God a name from stories like this: HaMakom, the Place. A midrash says God is the place of the world, but the world is not God's place. In other words, there's no spot on earth too plain for it. In Jacob's own words, God was already there; the dream didn't bring him. What changed was that he woke up and noticed.
screen: `A LADDER FROM EARTH TO HEAVEN.` · `I WILL BE WITH YOU WHEREVER YOU GO.` · `BETH-EL, THAT USED TO BE LUZ.` · `HAMAKOM: THE PLACE.` · then, large: `SURELY THE LORD IS IN THIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find God in a place you overlook. Settle, and breathe. Wherever you are right now, the car, a bench, the kitchen floor, look around slowly, as if you'd just woken from Jacob's dream. What's here that you've stopped seeing? The light on the wall. The sound of the street. The fact that you're breathing at all. If you pray, you can say Jacob's line quietly. If not, just let the place be more than it was a minute ago. The bell holds the time.
Vayetze. And he went out: the portion where Jacob sleeps on a stone in nowhere in particular, and wakes up saying God was there all along.
Your line: and I knew it not. Today, pick one overlooked place, a stairwell, a checkout line, and stop there for one breath, as if it were Beth-el. Day one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Jews often call God HaMakom, the Place, and the phrase appears in the traditional words of comfort said to mourners.

fork.setup: you wake up on a stone after a dream of angels on a ladder. you're Jacob. what do you say?
options: surely the LORD is in this place, and I knew it not.
I must build a city here.
fork.reveal: Jacob said God was in this place and he hadn't known it, and named it Beth-el, house of God.

original.note: Hebrew: and I knew it not. anochi is the long, heavy form of the word I.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dream about a ladder.
what it means: God was in an ordinary place all along; Jacob woke up and noticed.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah 68:9 explains the name HaMakom: God is the place of the world, and the world is not God's place.

sources.quoted: Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut superlatives ('the most unremarkable spot', 'a favorite image'); anochi described plainly; the 'God was already there' line now framed as Jacob's own words, not narrator fact.
Genesis 28:17 is paraphrased ('full of awe', 'house of God', 'gate of heaven'), not quoted.
The Hasidic reading of anochi (the ego kept him from knowing) is attributed only to 'some Hasidic teachers'; a Keeper may want a named source.
'Ascending then descending' noted in Genesis Rabbah 68:12 and Rashi on 28:12; confirm.
howItsDone: HaMakom in the words of comfort to mourners (HaMakom yenachem etchem); confirm.
